#[Fillable([
    'name', 'email', 'password', 'role', 'assigned_teacher_id', 'student_number', 'grade_level', 'section',
    'contact_number', 'address', 'guardian_name', 'guardian_relationship', 'guardian_contact_number',

#[Hidden(['password', 'remember_token'])]
class User extends Authenticatable

    {
        // Laravel hashes a password before it is saved to the database.
        return [
            'email_verified_at' => 'datetime',
            'password' => 'hashed',
        ];
    }

    public function appointmentsAsStudent(): HasMany
    {
        // Appointments where this user is the student receiving guidance.
        return $this->hasMany(Appointment::class, 'student_id');
    }

    public function assignedTeacher(): BelongsTo
    {
        // Teacher responsible for this student; null for accounts without an assignment.
        return $this->belongsTo(self::class, 'assigned_teacher_id');
    }

    public function assignedStudents(): HasMany
    {
        // Students linked to this teacher account.
        return $this->hasMany(self::class, 'assigned_teacher_id')->where('role', 'student');
    }

    public function appointmentsAssigned(): HasMany
    {
        // Consultations where this account is the assigned guidance administrator.
        return $this->hasMany(Appointment::class, 'assigned_to');
    }

    public function createdCases(): HasMany
    {
        // Case records authored by this account; used to preserve history on account deletion.
        return $this->hasMany(CaseRecord::class, 'created_by');
    }
}

<?php

namespace App\Providers;

use App\Actions\Fortify\CreateNewUser;
use App\Actions\Fortify\ResetUserPassword;
use App\Actions\Fortify\UpdateUserPassword;
use App\Actions\Fortify\UpdateUserProfileInformation;
use Illuminate\Cache\RateLimiting\Limit;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\RateLimiter;
use Illuminate\Support\ServiceProvider;
use Illuminate\Support\Str;
use Laravel\Fortify\Actions\RedirectIfTwoFactorAuthenticatable;
use Laravel\Fortify\Fortify;

class FortifyServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider
{
    /**
     * Register any application services.
     */
    public function register(): void
    {
        //
    }

    /**
     * Bootstrap any application services.
     */
    public function boot(): void
    {   
        Fortify::loginView(fn () => view('auth.login'));
        Fortify::createUsersUsing(CreateNewUser::class);
        Fortify::updateUserProfileInformationUsing(UpdateUserProfileInformation::class);
        Fortify::updateUserPasswordsUsing(UpdateUserPassword::class);
        Fortify::resetUserPasswordsUsing(ResetUserPassword::class);
        Fortify::redirectUserForTwoFactorAuthenticationUsing(RedirectIfTwoFactorAuthenticatable::class);

        RateLimiter::for('login', function (Request $request) {
            $throttleKey = Str::transliterate(Str::lower($request->input(Fortify::username())).'|'.$request->ip());

            return Limit::perMinute(5)->by($throttleKey);
        });

        RateLimiter::for('two-factor', function (Request $request) {
            return Limit::perMinute(5)->by($request->session()->get('login.id'));
        });

        RateLimiter::for('passkeys', function (Request $request) {
            $credentialId = $request->input('credential.id');

            return Limit::perMinute(10)->by(
                ($credentialId ?: $request->session()->getId()).'|'.$request->ip()
            );
        });
    }
}

<?php

use App\Http\Middleware\AppendMis215EggHeader;
use Illuminate\Auth\Access\AuthorizationException;
use Illuminate\Auth\AuthenticationException;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\ModelNotFoundException;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Exceptions;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Validation\ValidationException;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\HttpExceptionInterface;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\NotFoundHttpException;

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
        api: __DIR__.'/../routes/api.php',
        commands: __DIR__.'/../routes/console.php',
        health: '/up',
    )
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
        $middleware->web(append: [
            AppendMis215EggHeader::class,
        ]);
    })
    ->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions): void {
        $exceptions->shouldRenderJsonWhen(
            fn (Request $request) => $request->is('api/*') || $request->expectsJson(),
        );

        $exceptions->render(function (Throwable $exception, Request $request) {
            if (! $request->is('api/*')) {
                return null;
            }

            $status = match (true) {
                $exception instanceof ValidationException => 400,
                $exception instanceof AuthenticationException => 401,
                $exception instanceof AuthorizationException => 403,
                $exception instanceof ModelNotFoundException, $exception instanceof NotFoundHttpException => 404,
                $exception instanceof HttpExceptionInterface => $exception->getStatusCode() === 422
                    ? 400
                    : $exception->getStatusCode(),
                default => 500,
            };
            $code = match ($status) {
                400, 422 => 'BAD_REQUEST',
                401 => 'UNAUTHENTICATED',
                403 => 'FORBIDDEN',
                404 => 'NOT_FOUND',
                default => 'INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR',
            };
            $message = match ($status) {
                400, 422 => 'The request could not be processed.',
                401 => 'Authentication is required.',
                403 => 'You are not allowed to perform this action.',
                404 => 'The requested resource was not found.',
                default => 'An unexpected server error occurred.',
            };

            $body = ['error' => ['code' => $code, 'message' => $message]];
            if ($exception instanceof ValidationException) {
                $body['error']['details'] = $exception->errors();
            }

            $response = response()->json($body, $status);
            if ($status === 401) {
                $response->headers->set('WWW-Authenticate', 'Basic realm="GuidanceSched API"');
            }

            return $response;
        });
    })->create();

    | reset "broker" for your application. You may change these values

    |
    */

        'guard' => env('AUTH_GUARD', 'web'),
        'passwords' => env('AUTH_PASSWORD_BROKER', 'users'),
    ],

    /*
    |--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    | Authentication Guards
    |--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    |
    | Next, you may define every authentication guard for your application.
    | Of course, a great default configuration has been defined for you
    | which utilizes session storage plus the Eloquent user provider.
    |
    | All authentication guards have a user provider, which defines how the
    | users are actually retrieved out of your database or other storage
    | system used by the application. Typically, Eloquent is utilized.
    |
    | Supported: "session"
    |
    */

    'guards' => [
        'web' => [
            'driver' => 'session',
            'provider' => 'users',
        ],
    ],

    /*
    |--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    | User Providers
    |--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    |
    | All authentication guards have a user provider, which defines how the
    | users are actually retrieved out of your database or other storage
    | system used by the application. Typically, Eloquent is utilized.
    |
    | If you have multiple user tables or models you may configure multiple
    | providers to represent the model / table. These providers may then
    | be assigned to any extra authentication guards you have defined.
    |
    | Supported: "database", "eloquent"
    |
    */

    'providers' => [
        'users' => [
            'driver' => 'eloquent',
            'model' => env('AUTH_MODEL', User::class),
        ],

        // 'users' => [
        //     'driver' => 'database',
        //     'table' => 'users',
        // ],
    ],

    /*
    |--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    | Resetting Passwords
    |--------------------------------------------------------------------------
    |
    | These configuration options specify the behavior of Laravel's password
    | reset functionality, including the table utilized for token storage
    | and the user provider that is invoked to actually retrieve users.
    |
    | The expiry time is the number of minutes that each reset token will be
    | considered valid. This security feature keeps tokens short-lived so
    | they have less time to be guessed. You may change this as needed.
    |
    | The throttle setting is the number of seconds a user must wait before
    | generating more password reset tokens. This prevents the user from
    | quickly generating a very large amount of password reset tokens.
    |
    */

    'passwords' => [
        'users' => [
            'provider' => 'users',
            'table' => env('AUTH_PASSWORD_RESET_TOKEN_TABLE', 'password_reset_tokens'),
            'expire' => 60,
            'throttle' => 60,
        ],
    ],

<?php

namespace Database\Factories;

use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Factories\Factory;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Hash;
use Illuminate\Support\Str;

/**
 * @extends Factory<User>
 */
class UserFactory extends Factory
{
    /**
     * The current password being used by the factory.
     */
    protected static ?string $password;

    /**
     * Define the model's default state.
     *
     * @return array<string, mixed>
     */
    public function definition(): array
    {
        return [
            'name' => fake()->name(),
            'email' => fake()->unique()->safeEmail(),
            'email_verified_at' => now(),
            'password' => static::$password ??= Hash::make('password'),
            'remember_token' => Str::random(10),
        ];
    }

    /**
     * Indicate that the model's email address should be unverified.
     */
    public function unverified(): static
    {
        return $this->state(fn (array $attributes) => [
            'email_verified_at' => null,
        ]);
    }
}

FILE: database/seeders/LoadTestDataSeeder.php

<?php

namespace Database\Seeders;

use App\Models\Appointment;
use App\Models\CaseRecord;
use App\Models\FollowUp;
use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\Database\Seeder;
use Illuminate\Support\Carbon;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Hash;
use InvalidArgumentException;
use RuntimeException;

class LoadTestDataSeeder extends Seeder
{
    public function run(): void
    {
        // Avoid accidentally inserting a large synthetic dataset into a live database.
        if (app()->environment('production') && ! filter_var(env('LOAD_TEST_ALLOW_PRODUCTION', false), FILTER_VALIDATE_BOOLEAN)) {
            throw new RuntimeException('Load-test seeding is disabled in production. Set LOAD_TEST_ALLOW_PRODUCTION=true only for a controlled test.');
        }

        // Counts can be increased in the local .env to match the scale of a planned load test.
        $teacherCount = $this->positiveCount('LOAD_TEST_TEACHERS', 10);
        $studentCount = $this->positiveCount('LOAD_TEST_STUDENTS', 250);
        $appointmentCount = $this->positiveCount('LOAD_TEST_APPOINTMENTS', 2000);
        $caseCount = $this->positiveCount('LOAD_TEST_CASES', 500);
        $followUpsPerCase = $this->positiveCount('LOAD_TEST_FOLLOW_UPS_PER_CASE', 2);

        $admin = User::query()->where('role', 'admin')->firstOrFail();
        $password = Hash::make((string) env('LOAD_TEST_PASSWORD', 'LoadTestPass123!'));

        // Stable email keys let reruns update the same test accounts instead of creating duplicates.
        $teachers = collect(range(1, $teacherCount))->map(function (int $number) use ($password): User {
            return User::query()->updateOrCreate(
                ['email' => sprintf('loadtest.teacher.%04d@guidancesched.test', $number)],
                [
                    'name' => sprintf('Load Test Teacher %04d', $number),
                    'role' => 'teacher',
                    'password' => $password,
                ],
            );
        })->values();

        $students = collect(range(1, $studentCount))->map(function (int $number) use ($teachers, $password): User {
            $teacher = $teachers[($number - 1) % $teachers->count()];

            return User::query()->updateOrCreate(
                ['email' => sprintf('loadtest.student.%05d@guidancesched.test', $number)],
                [
                    'name' => sprintf('Load Test Student %05d', $number),
                    'role' => 'student',
                    'password' => $password,
                    'student_number' => sprintf('LOAD-%06d', $number),
                    'grade_level' => sprintf('Grade %d', (($number - 1) % 6) + 7),
                    'section' => sprintf('Synthetic Section %02d', (($number - 1) % 12) + 1),
                    'assigned_teacher_id' => $teacher->id,
                ],
            );
        })->values();

        // Distribute requests across the generated students and teachers, cycling through every status.
        $appointments = collect(range(1, $appointmentCount))->map(function (int $number) use ($admin, $students, $teachers): Appointment {
            $student = $students[($number - 1) % $students->count()];
            $teacher = $teachers[($number - 1) % $teachers->count()];
            $status = Appointment::STATUSES[($number - 1) % count(Appointment::STATUSES)];
            $scheduledAt = in_array($status, ['pending', 'approved'], true)
                ? now()->addDays(($number % 60) + 1)->setTime(8 + ($number % 8), ($number % 2) * 30)
                : now()->subDays(($number % 180) + 1)->setTime(8 + ($number % 8), ($number % 2) * 30);

            return Appointment::query()->updateOrCreate(
                [
                    'student_id' => $student->id,
                    'title' => sprintf('Load-test consultation %06d', $number),
                ],
                [
                    'created_by' => $teacher->id,
                    'assigned_to' => $admin->id,
                    'reason' => 'Synthetic load-test reason. No real person or case is represented.',
                    'scheduled_at' => $scheduledAt,
                    'duration_minutes' => 30,
                    'status' => $status,
                    'notes' => 'Synthetic load-test note.',
                ],
            );
        })->values();

        // Give generated cases links to generated students and appointments for realistic list/detail queries.
        $cases = collect(range(1, $caseCount))->map(function (int $number) use ($admin, $students, $appointments): CaseRecord {
            $studentIndex = ($number - 1) % $students->count();
            $appointment = $appointments[($number - 1) % $appointments->count()];

            return CaseRecord::query()->updateOrCreate(
                ['case_number' => sprintf('LOADTEST-%06d', $number)],
                [
                    'student_id' => $students[$studentIndex]->id,
                    'created_by' => $admin->id,
                    'appointment_id' => $appointment->id,
                    'title' => sprintf('Synthetic support case %06d', $number),
                    'description' => 'Synthetic load-test description. No real person or confidential information is represented.',
                    'status' => ['open', 'in_progress', 'closed'][($number - 1) % 3],
                    'category' => ['academic', 'behavioral', 'personal'][($number - 1) % 3],
                ],
            );
        })->values();

        // Anchor follow-up dates to the case creation date so rerunning the seeder keeps the same keys.
        foreach ($cases as $caseIndex => $case) {
            for ($followUpNumber = 1; $followUpNumber <= $followUpsPerCase; $followUpNumber++) {
                $date = Carbon::parse($case->created_at)->subDays($followUpNumber * 7 + ($caseIndex % 30))->toDateString();

                FollowUp::query()->updateOrCreate(
                    [
                        'case_record_id' => $case->id,
                        'follow_up_date' => $date,
                    ],
                    [
                        'created_by' => $case->created_by,
                        'notes' => 'Synthetic load-test follow-up. No real person or confidential information is represented.',
                        'action_taken' => 'Recorded synthetic follow-up',
                    ],
                );
            }
        }

        $this->command?->info(sprintf(
            'Synthetic load-test data ready: %d teachers, %d students, %d appointments, %d cases, and up to %d follow-ups.',
            $teachers->count(),
            $students->count(),
            $appointments->count(),
            $cases->count(),
            $cases->count() * $followUpsPerCase,
        ));
    }

    private function positiveCount(string $environmentVariable, int $default): int
    {
        // A zero/negative count could leave later records without teachers, students, or parent rows.
        $count = (int) env($environmentVariable, $default);

        if ($count < 1) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException(sprintf('%s must be a positive integer.', $environmentVariable));
        }

        return $count;
    }
}

# API test plan and run record

Base URL: `http://localhost` (replace with the app's actual local URL). Run `vendor/bin/sail artisan db:seed` first. Demo credentials are `admin@guidancesched.test` / `ChangeMe123!`, `teacher@guidancesched.test` / `ChangeMe123!`, and `student@guidancesched.test` / `ChangeMe123!`. Seeded case ID and appointment ID can be looked up in the database; use `CASE_ID` and `APPOINTMENT_ID` below. To obtain a student id for appointment creation, query the seeded student by email and set `STUDENT_ID`.

All commands use curl and `-i` so the HTTP status is captured. Each route has one success and one failure check. Failure checks expect the common body `{"error":{"code":"...","message":"..."}}`; request validation errors use HTTP 400 and may also include `details`. A failure status differing from the expected result should be recorded as failed.

## Endpoint cases

| # | Endpoint | Success | Failure | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `GET /api/appointments` | `curl -i -u student@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! http://localhost/api/appointments` → 200 | `curl -i http://localhost/api/appointments` → 401 `UNAUTHENTICATED` | Not run: Sail reports Docker/Podman is not running |
| 2 | `POST /api/appointments` | `curl -i -u admin@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"student_id\":$STUDENT_ID,\"title\":\"API test request\"}" http://localhost/api/appointments` → 201 | `curl -i -u admin@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"student_id\":$STUDENT_ID}" http://localhost/api/appointments` → 400 `BAD_REQUEST` | Not run: Sail reports Docker/Podman is not running |
| 3 | `GET /api/appointments/{appointment}` | `curl -i -u student@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! http://localhost/api/appointments/$APPOINTMENT_ID` → 200 | `curl -i -u admin@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! http://localhost/api/appointments/99999999` → 404 `NOT_FOUND` | Not run: Sail reports Docker/Podman is not running |
| 4 | `PATCH /api/appointments/{appointment}` | `curl -i -u student@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! -X PATCH -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Updated API request"}' http://localhost/api/appointments/$APPOINTMENT_ID` → 200 | Same command with `-d '{}'` → 400 `BAD_REQUEST` | Not run: Sail reports Docker/Podman is not running |
| 5 | `PATCH /api/appointments/{appointment}/cancel` | `curl -i -u admin@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! -X PATCH http://localhost/api/appointments/$APPOINTMENT_ID/cancel` → 200 | Student credentials on the same request → 403 `FORBIDDEN` | Not run: Sail reports Docker/Podman is not running |
| 6 | `DELETE /api/appointments/{appointment}` | `curl -i -u admin@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! -X DELETE http://localhost/api/appointments/$APPOINTMENT_ID` → 204 with no body; verify the row is gone | Student credentials on the same request → 403 `FORBIDDEN` | Not run: Sail reports Docker/Podman is not running |
| 7 | `GET /api/cases` | `curl -i -u admin@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! http://localhost/api/cases` → 200 | `curl -i -u student@guidancesched.test:ChangeMe123! http://localhost/api/cases` → 403 `FORBIDDEN` | Not run: Sail reports Docker/Podman is not running |

# GuidanceSched: presentation outline

Use this outline to explain the system in 11 slides. It is based on the project files. Any proposed improvements are labeled as recommendations. No load-test results are available yet.

## 1. Title

**GuidanceSched**  
A school guidance appointment and case-record system  
How it works, how it is set up, and how it protects information

Presenter: [Name] · School: [School] · Date: [Date]

## 2. Organization and problem

- **Organization:** a school guidance center that arranges student consultations and follow-up.
- **Problem:** appointment requests, student details, private case records, and follow-up notes can be hard to keep organized when tracked separately.
- **What the system does:** helps staff manage appointments, accounts, case records, and follow-ups. It also provides different pages for different users and a few ways for other programs to exchange data with it.
- **Project limit:** this is a school project prototype. It has not had a formal school privacy review and is not ready to be described as a production counseling system.

## 3. Users and main tasks

| User | What they can do |
| --- | --- |
| Admin / guidance staff | Manage accounts; schedule, approve, complete, or cancel appointments; view and update case records; add follow-up notes |
| Teacher | Work with assigned students; create consultation requests and set available times; view related appointments |
| Student | View their own assigned consultation date, time, and status; staff create requests for them |

Main tasks:

1. A staff member creates an appointment request for a student.
2. A teacher sets a time, or an admin schedules and approves it.
3. Staff records a case and can add follow-up notes later.
4. An admin manages user accounts.

## 4. Three main parts of the system

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph P[Part 1: What users see]
    B[Web pages in a browser]
    C[Other programs using the API]
  end
  subgraph A[Part 2: What processes requests]
    R[Laravel routes and login checks]
    CT[Controllers: check and handle requests]
    M[Models: work with the system's data]
  end
  subgraph D[Part 3: Where information is stored]
    PG[(PostgreSQL database)]
  end
  B -->|Web requests and pages| R
  C -->|Requests and JSON data| R
  R --> CT --> M --> PG
```

- **Part 1 — What users see:** web pages in a browser. Other programs can also use the system through its API, a few web addresses for exchanging information.
- **Part 2 — What processes requests:** the Laravel app checks who is signed in, checks what they are allowed to do, and handles their request.
- **Part 3 — Where information is stored:** the PostgreSQL database saves users, appointments, case records, and follow-ups.
- These are three parts of how the system works. They are not three separate apps: the current setup runs one Laravel app and one database.

## 5. How a teacher schedules an appointment

Example: a teacher sends an appointment request with a chosen time.

1. The teacher submits a form on a web page or sends a request through the API.
2. The Laravel app receives the request.
3. It checks that the teacher is signed in and allowed to work with that student.
4. It checks that the student and time are valid and that the time is available.
5. The app saves the appointment as **pending**, with the student, teacher, and time. The default appointment length is 30 minutes.
6. The database saves the appointment. The system then shows an updated page or sends back a result to the API user.
7. An admin can later approve, complete, or cancel the appointment.

The system can reject a request if the user is not signed in (API: 401), is not allowed to do it (403), or entered invalid information (422).

## 6. How parts of the system communicate

| Connection | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Browser to app | The browser sends a web request and receives a page. Users sign in to the website. Use HTTPS, the secure form of web traffic, when people connect over a network. |
| Other program to app | A program can use the API to send or receive information as JSON, a simple text format computers use to share data. It signs in with an existing account. Use HTTPS when sending login details over a network. |
| App to database | The app sends database requests over the private Docker network. Database login details come from settings outside the source code. |

- The API shows lists in smaller pages of results. It returns JSON data and uses error codes when something goes wrong.
- Students see only limited information about their own appointments. Only admins can use the case and follow-up API addresses.
- The API uses Basic Authentication, a simple sign-in method. Before real use, the school should review whether a stronger sign-in method is needed.

### Communication protocol specification (summary)

GuidanceSched exposes a REST-style API under `/api`. Clients send and receive JSON over HTTP; use **HTTPS** whenever traffic crosses a network so credentials and student information are encrypted in transit. The checked-in development setup may use local HTTP, so it should not be treated as a secure public deployment. Every API endpoint requires HTTP Basic Authentication, and the server applies role and record-level access checks. Case and follow-up endpoints are administrator-only.

| Core transaction | Endpoint | Method | Access |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List appointments | `/api/appointments` | GET | Signed-in users; results scoped by role |
| Create appointment request | `/api/appointments` | POST | Admin or teacher |
| Read appointment | `/api/appointments/{appointment}` | GET | Authorized owner or staff |
| Update appointment | `/api/appointments/{appointment}` | PATCH | Authorized staff; fields depend on role/state |
| Cancel appointment | `/api/appointments/{appointment}/cancel` | PATCH | Admin |
| Delete appointment | `/api/appointments/{appointment}` | DELETE | Admin |
| List / read cases | `/api/cases`, `/api/cases/{case}` | GET | Admin |
| Change case status | `/api/cases/{case}/status` | PATCH | Admin |
| List / record follow-ups | `/api/cases/{case}/follow-ups` | GET / POST | Admin |

Successful reads and updates return **200**, new records return **201**, and deletes return **204** with no response body. Errors use a consistent JSON object, for example `{"error":{"code":"BAD_REQUEST","message":"The request could not be processed.","details":{"title":["The title field is required."]}}}`. The API uses **400** for invalid input, **401** for missing or invalid credentials, **403** for insufficient permissions, **404** for missing or inaccessible records, and **500** for unexpected server errors.

## Appendix A. Full communication protocol specification

The machine-readable **OpenAPI 3.0.3** specification is in [`docs/openapi.yaml`](openapi.yaml). It defines the endpoint URIs, HTTP methods, request and response formats, authentication, and possible status codes for all 11 operations listed above. It is the full endpoint reference for this summary.

The endpoint-by-endpoint curl success and failure cases are in [`docs/api-test-plan.md`](api-test-plan.md). They are prepared but have **not been executed** because the local Docker/Podman service was unavailable when checked. Record actual HTTP results there after running the application; the listed cases are not evidence of successful execution.

All error responses use `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "...", "details": { ... } } }`. `details` is included for validation errors when field-level information is available. Authentication is required for every operation. The API's common status codes are 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, and 500; route-specific responses are documented in the OpenAPI file.

## 7. Where the system runs

| Area | Deployment |
| --- | --- |
| Environment | Development runs in WSL Ubuntu with Docker Desktop. A temporary online test deployment is defined for Render in Singapore. |
| Containers | Docker Compose runs the PHP 8.5 Laravel app and PostgreSQL 18 locally. Render builds the app image from `Dockerfile` and connects it to a managed PostgreSQL database. |
| Virtual machines | No project-specific virtual machine is configured. Docker Desktop and Render provide the underlying host infrastructure. |
| Network access | Locally, the browser reaches the app on the host's web port; the app and database communicate over a private Docker network. PostgreSQL is bound to localhost only. On Render, users reach the web service at its HTTPS URL and the app connects to the database over Render's private network. |

The Render setup is for testing, not production. Before shared use, review HTTPS, secret settings, database access, backups, monitoring, and the school's privacy requirements. Use synthetic records until the school approves real data use.

## 8. Data design and storage plan

GuidanceSched uses PostgreSQL, a relational database management system, as the authoritative store for business data. The local Docker Compose setup runs PostgreSQL 18. The core entities are users, appointments, case records, and follow-ups. Foreign keys connect records and define what happens when a related record is deleted.

### Entity-relationship diagram

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ USERS : "assigned teacher"
    USERS ||--o{ APPOINTMENTS : "student"
    USERS ||--o{ APPOINTMENTS : "creates"
    USERS ||--o{ APPOINTMENTS : "assigned staff"
    APPOINTMENTS ||--o{ CASE_RECORDS : "optional link"
    USERS ||--o{ CASE_RECORDS : "student"
    USERS ||--o{ CASE_RECORDS : "creates"
    CASE_RECORDS ||--o{ FOLLOW_UPS : "has"
    USERS ||--o{ FOLLOW_UPS : "creates"
    USERS ||--o{ PASSKEYS : "registers"

    USERS {
        bigint id PK
        string email UK
        string role
        bigint assigned_teacher_id FK
        string student_number UK
    }
    APPOINTMENTS {
        bigint id PK
        bigint student_id FK
        bigint created_by FK
        bigint assigned_to FK
        datetime scheduled_at
        string status
    }
    CASE_RECORDS {
        bigint id PK
        bigint student_id FK
        bigint created_by FK
        bigint appointment_id FK
        string case_number UK
        string status
    }
    FOLLOW_UPS {
        bigint id PK
        bigint case_record_id FK
        bigint created_by FK
        date follow_up_date
        text notes
    }
    PASSKEYS {
        bigint id PK
        bigint user_id FK
        string credential_id UK
        json credential
    }
```

`PK` means primary key, `FK` means foreign key, and `UK` means unique value. Laravel also defines support tables for sessions, password resets, caching, and queued jobs.

### Data dictionary

| Table | Important fields | Purpose and relationships |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `users` | `id`, `name`, `email`, `password`, `role`, `student_number`, `grade_level`, `section`, contact and guardian fields, `assigned_teacher_id` | Student, teacher, and administrator accounts. `assigned_teacher_id` optionally relates a student to a teacher in this table. Email and student number are unique. Passwords are stored as hashes. |
| `appointments` | `id`, `student_id`, `created_by`, `assigned_to`, `title`, `reason`, `scheduled_at`, `duration_minutes`, `status`, `notes` | A consultation request for a student, created by an account and optionally assigned to staff. `notes` are staff-only. Student deletion cascades to appointments; deleting creator or assignee accounts clears those references. |
| `case_records` | `id`, `student_id`, `created_by`, `appointment_id`, `case_number`, `title`, `description`, `status`, `category`, `remarks`, session date/time, `findings`, `recommendations` | Confidential guidance case linked to a student and creator, optionally linked to an appointment. Case number is unique. Deleting a student deletes their cases; deleting a linked appointment clears the optional link. |
| `follow_ups` | `id`, `case_record_id`, `created_by`, `follow_up_date`, `notes`, `action_taken` | Dated actions and notes belonging to a case. Deleting a case cascades to its follow-ups. Creator account deletion is restricted to preserve attribution. |
| `passkeys` | `id`, `user_id`, `name`, `credential_id`, `credential`, `last_used_at` | Authentication credentials associated with a user account. Deleting the account deletes its passkeys. |
| `sessions` | `id`, `user_id`, `ip_address`, `user_agent`, `payload`, `last_activity` | Laravel browser session data. `.env.example` selects the database session driver, so the session table is used with that configuration. |
| Support tables | `password_reset_tokens`, `cache`, `cache_locks`, `jobs`, `job_batches`, `failed_jobs` | Framework support for password resets, cache, and queued work. |

### Client-side storage

The browser does not store business records such as appointments, profiles, cases, or follow-up notes locally. Those remain on the server in PostgreSQL. Browser authentication uses a session cookie, while session state is managed server-side according to the Laravel session configuration. Do not put student information, passwords, or authentication tokens in browser local storage.

### Backup and restore procedure

Backups contain sensitive student information. Keep them access-controlled, encrypted when stored or transferred, and outside source control. Run these scripts from the project root while Sail's PostgreSQL service is running. Use a separate, disposable database for restore verification.

**Backup script** (`backup-guidancesched.sh`):

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

backup_file="${1:-backups/guidancesched-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).dump}"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$backup_file")"

vendor/bin/sail exec -T pgsql sh -c \
  'pg_dump -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" --format=custom' \
  > "$backup_file"

chmod 600 "$backup_file"
printf 'Backup created: %s\n' "$backup_file"
```

**Restore script** (`restore-guidancesched.sh`):

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

backup_file="${1:?Usage: restore-guidancesched.sh BACKUP_FILE}"
test -r "$backup_file"
restore_db="guidancesched_restore_test"

# This dedicated test database is recreated on each run; the configured app database is untouched.
vendor/bin/sail exec -T pgsql sh -c \
  'dropdb --if-exists -U "$POSTGRES_USER" guidancesched_restore_test && createdb -U "$POSTGRES_USER" guidancesched_restore_test'

vendor/bin/sail exec -T pgsql sh -c \
  'pg_restore --no-owner -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d guidancesched_restore_test' \
  < "$backup_file"

vendor/bin/sail exec -T pgsql sh -c \
  'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d guidancesched_restore_test -c "\\dt"'

printf 'Restored %s into %s; verify expected tables and synthetic records before removing the test database.\n' "$backup_file" "$restore_db"
```

After restoring, check that expected tables and known synthetic records exist, then confirm the restored data can be read by the application or a test connection. Record the backup date, restore date, target test database, and verification result. The test database and backup must be protected and removed securely when the drill is complete.

**Restore demonstration:** Not yet recorded. Run the scripts against the local Sail database and replace this note with the observed result. A successful `pg_restore` command alone is not enough; verify expected tables and records.

The school still needs to set its retention and deletion schedule and decide how often backups are taken, where protected copies are stored, and who may restore them.

## 9. Security and student privacy (RA 10173)

- RA 10173, the Data Privacy Act of 2012, says personal information must be handled with transparency, for a proper purpose, and only as much as needed. See the [National Privacy Commission's copy of the law](https://privacy.gov.ph/data-privacy-act/).
- **Already in the project:** users must sign in; the app checks user roles and access; only admins can view case and follow-up records; forms check the information entered; passwords are saved in protected form; students see limited appointment details; anyone cannot sign themselves up.
- **Private information in the system:** student and guardian details, appointment reasons, case descriptions, findings, recommendations, and follow-up notes.
- **Before using real student information:** the school should explain why it collects information, who can see it, how it is protected, and when it is deleted. Use secure connections, protect backups, review staff access, and plan what to do if information is exposed.
- These system features do not prove that the school follows the law. Ask the school's Data Protection Officer to review the system before using real student records. Use made-up records for demos.

## 10. Checking speed and comparing designs

**Speed test status:** the project has no recorded test results. Run the test with made-up data before presenting any speed numbers.

When testing, record:

- Date, PHP and database versions, and computer or server used.
- Which page or API address was tested, how many requests were sent, and how many at once.
- How many requests succeeded or failed, how long they took, and how many requests finished per second.
- Repeat the test and note whether the app had already been used recently.

Suggested small test: request the appointment list 100 times, with 5 requests at once, using the made-up admin account. This is only a basic check, not proof the system can handle a large school. Do not test with real student information or on a shared live system without approval.

| Design | Possible benefit | Possible cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current design: one Laravel app and one database | Easier to set up and maintain for a small project; related changes can be saved together | If more capacity is needed, the app is scaled as a whole; all features share one release |
| Split the system into several apps | Each app could be changed or scaled separately | More pieces to set up, connect, secure, and monitor; keeping information in sync is harder |

To compare the designs, test the same tasks on the same computer or server. Compare speed, errors, computer use, ease of maintenance, and whether information stays consistent. No such comparison has been run yet; the table lists expected trade-offs only.

## 11. Limits and next steps

**Current limits**

- This is a prototype and has not had a formal school privacy review.
- No speed test or design comparison results have been recorded.
- The API sign-in and local Docker setup need review before shared or real use.
- The school has not set record-keeping time limits or a full plan for monitoring and responding to problems.
- The local setup does not include a complete plan for keeping a live service available or recovering from a major failure.

**Next steps**

1. Ask school staff and the Data Protection Officer to review the work process, information collected, who can see it, and when it should be deleted.
2. Review sign-in, secure connections, passwords and secret settings, activity records, and how access is checked.
3. Write down how to back up and restore information and respond to a security problem.
4. Run and record speed tests using made-up records.
5. Try the system with made-up records first. Use real student information only after school approval.

# Data Privacy Compliance Note

**System:** GuidanceSched  
**Applicable law:** Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173)  
**Status:** Academic prototype. Use synthetic, non-identifying data only until the school has reviewed and approved real-data use.

## 1. Purpose and privacy principles

GuidanceSched is a school guidance workflow prototype for user accounts, student consultations, guidance case records, and follow-up actions. Its intended use is to help authorized school personnel coordinate consultations and maintain relevant guidance records. It does not make automated decisions about students.

The system should be used according to the Data Privacy Act’s principles of transparency, legitimate purpose, and proportionality. Information should be collected only when needed for a stated school function, used only for that function, and made available only to people who need it for their duties. This note describes the prototype and its current limitations; it is not a certification of legal compliance or approval to process actual student information. The school is responsible for confirming its authority, policies, and safeguards before deployment. ([RA 10173, Sections 11–13](https://privacy.gov.ph/data-privacy-act/))

## 2. Personal data collected and purposes

The application stores the following categories of information to support its workflows:

| Data category | Examples | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account and authentication data | Name, email address, role, password hash, and session information | Identify users, authenticate sign-in, administer accounts, and maintain a signed-in session. Passwords are stored as hashes rather than readable text. |
| Student and school details | Student number, grade level, section, address, contact number, assigned teacher | Identify a student, support school contact, and associate the student with the appropriate teacher and guidance workflow. |
| Parent or guardian details | Name, relationship to the student, and contact number | Support appropriate school contact when needed for the guidance process. |
| Consultation and appointment data | Student and staff links, title, reason, proposed or scheduled date and time, duration, status, and staff notes | Request, assign, schedule, and track consultations. Reasons and staff notes may reveal sensitive personal information depending on what is entered. |
| Guidance case and follow-up data | Case title and category, description, dates, remarks, findings, recommendations, follow-up notes, and actions | Document a guidance case and coordinate follow-up by authorized personnel. These records may contain sensitive personal information. |
| Technical request information | Information needed to process a website or API request and maintain a session | Operate, secure, and troubleshoot the service. The prototype does not describe a comprehensive activity audit trail. |

Users should not enter unnecessary details into free-text fields. In particular, sensitive information should not be included unless the school has approved the purpose, access, and handling rules for it. The prototype is intended for synthetic records and should not be populated with real student, family, or case details at this stage.

## 3. Lawful basis for processing

For current demonstrations, synthetic data is used; this note does not establish a lawful basis for processing real personal data. Before real-data use, the school, as the proposed personal information controller, must determine and document the applicable lawful condition for each purpose. The Data Privacy Act requires a condition under Section 12 for personal information and an applicable condition under Section 13 for sensitive personal information. Guidance notes may include information covered by the sensitive-personal-information rules.

The correct basis depends on the school’s status, the specific activity, applicable education laws and policies, and the individuals concerned. The school must also determine what authority applies when processing information about minors. Consent should not automatically be treated as the basis for every school record; the basis must be assessed for the actual purpose and circumstances. The school’s Data Protection Officer (DPO) or privacy officer should review and document this assessment and approve the privacy notice before any real student or family information is entered. ([RA 10173, Sections 12–13](https://privacy.gov.ph/data-privacy-act/))

## 4. Access and access control

Access requires a user account and sign-in. Server-side role and record checks restrict what authenticated users can view or change; hiding an option in the interface is not the only control. Current application roles have these broad permissions:

- **Administrators / guidance personnel:** manage user accounts and access consultation, case, and follow-up workflows. Case and follow-up records are restricted to administrators.
- **Teachers:** work with students assigned to them and related consultation workflows. Their access is limited by assignment and role checks.
- **Students:** view their own assigned consultation date, time, and status. They cannot access guidance case notes. Student-facing appointment responses omit internal staff notes.

Accounts and assignments should be issued to named individuals, with access limited to the duties they perform. The school should remove or adjust access promptly when roles change, periodically review active accounts and teacher-student assignments, and prohibit shared accounts. The prototype does not provide a comprehensive record-access audit trail, so access review and accountability procedures require additional school processes.

## 5. Retention and disposal

The prototype has no automatic retention schedule or expiry-based deletion. For class demonstrations and evaluation, retain only synthetic data for the period needed to complete the activity. At the end, an operator should remove the demonstration database and dataset exports, screenshots, and any backups that contain the data, then confirm that the demo instance no longer holds those copies.

For real records, the school must approve a retention schedule for each record type, taking account of the original purpose and applicable education, archival, and other legal requirements. Keep identifiable records only as long as necessary or legally required. At the end of the approved period, securely erase or irreversibly anonymize the records. Backup copies should be removed according to an approved backup rotation and disposal procedure. Disposal should be documented by the responsible person. No fixed retention period is stated here because the school’s schedule has not been supplied. ([NPC Implementing Rules and Regulations](https://privacy.gov.ph/implementing-rules-regulations-data-privacy-act-2012/))

## 6. Security measures and relationship to R4

The prototype includes several controls relevant to the security measures described in **R4**:

- Authentication is required for protected application functions; there is no public self-registration flow.
- Server-side role and ownership or assignment checks limit access to records.
- Passwords are stored as hashes, and application forms validate submitted values and use CSRF protection.
- Student-facing consultation responses limit displayed information and omit internal staff notes.
- The local application and database communicate through a private Docker network, with the database bound to localhost in the development setup.

These measures help with access control, credential protection, input handling, and limiting disclosure. They do not by themselves make the prototype suitable for real student records. The local development setup may use HTTP and has not verified production HTTPS, protected secrets, least-privilege production database credentials, encryption at rest, monitored security logs, backup rotation, or a tested incident-response process. A comprehensive access audit trail is also not demonstrated. Before real-data use, the school and deployment operator must configure and verify secure connections, database and backup protections, account and access reviews, monitoring, restoration procedures, and incident reporting and response. This aligns with the Act’s requirement for reasonable and appropriate organizational, physical, and technical safeguards. ([RA 10173, Section 20](https://privacy.gov.ph/data-privacy-act/))

## 7. Data subject access and correction

The current prototype has no student self-service feature to download or edit personal data. A student, or a parent or guardian where legally authorized, should contact the school office or DPO using the contact information in the school’s approved privacy notice. The school must publish its controller and DPO contact details and request procedure before collecting real information.

When a request is received, the school should verify the requester’s identity and, where applicable, their authority to act for the student. It should locate the relevant records, provide the requester secure access to information they are entitled to receive, and correct inaccurate or incomplete data through an authorized staff member. The response should avoid disclosing another person’s information. Corrections to guidance notes may require review by authorized personnel and should follow the school’s record-history policy. The school should keep only the request documentation needed for accountability and handle the request within the applicable legal and school-policy timeframes. ([RA 10173, Section 16](https://privacy.gov.ph/data-privacy-act/); [NPC: Data Subject Rights](https://privacy.gov.ph/data-subject-rights/))

## 8. Review and approval before real-data use

Before deployment with real student or family information, the school should have its DPO or privacy officer review this note, confirm the lawful basis and retention schedule, approve the privacy notice and access policy, and verify the R4 security measures in the intended hosting environment. Until that review and approval are complete, use synthetic data only.

**Review date:** ____________________  **Approval date:** ____________________

# How GuidanceSched was built and how to try it

This guide explains the project in plain language, using WSL Ubuntu, Docker Desktop, PostgreSQL, Laravel, and Render.

## 1. What each tool does

- **WSL + Ubuntu:** your Linux workspace inside Windows. Keep the project in Ubuntu's files, such as `~/projects/GuidanceSched`, instead of under `/mnt/c` for better Docker performance.
- **Docker Desktop:** runs containers, which are separate boxes for software.
- **Docker Compose:** starts the app box and database box together and connects them.
- **Laravel:** the PHP app that shows web pages, checks sign-ins, applies rules, and saves information.
- **PostgreSQL:** the database that stores accounts, appointments, cases, and follow-ups.
- **Render:** builds the Docker image from GitHub and runs it online with a separate PostgreSQL database.

## 2. How this website was put together

1. **Define the users and tasks.** The project has admin/guidance staff, teachers, and students, each with different access.
2. **Create the Laravel app.** Laravel handles web pages, sign-in, form checks, and the rules for who can view or change records.
3. **Create the database tables.** Migrations describe the PostgreSQL tables for users, appointments, cases, follow-ups, and web sessions.
4. **Connect pages and data.** Routes send each browser or API request to a controller. Controllers check the user and request, then Laravel models read or update PostgreSQL.
5. **Add the web pages and API.** Blade is Laravel's tool for making pages shown in a browser. The API is a small set of web addresses other programs can use to exchange data in JSON, a simple text format.
6. **Put the app and database in Docker.** `compose.yaml` describes the local app and PostgreSQL containers. `Dockerfile` describes how to build the app container for local or online use.
7. **Add made-up demo records.** The local database seeder creates fictional accounts and example data. The online container does not run the seeder automatically, so it cannot publish the repository's known demo passwords.

## 3. Prepare WSL Ubuntu and Docker Desktop

1. Install Docker Desktop for Windows and enable **Settings → Resources → WSL Integration** for your Ubuntu distribution.
2. Open Ubuntu and check Docker is available:

   ```bash
   docker --version
   docker compose version
   ```

3. Install Git, PHP **8.4.1 or later**, Composer, and the PHP extensions Composer requests. This project cannot run with PHP 8.1. Check versions:

   ```bash
   php -v
   composer -V
   ```

4. Put the project in Ubuntu's Linux home directory, for example `~/projects/GuidanceSched`, then open that folder in the Ubuntu terminal.
5. Make sure the repository files are available there. If cloning for the first time:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/projects
   cd ~/projects
   git clone https://github.com/duranafloramaesanchez/GuidanceSched.git
   cd GuidanceSched
   ```

## 4. Start the website locally

Run these from the project folder in Ubuntu:

1. Install the PHP packages first. This creates the Sail files that the Compose setup uses:

   ```bash
   composer install
   ```

2. Create your local settings file:

   ```bash
   cp .env.example .env
   ```

   In `.env`, keep `DB_CONNECTION=pgsql` and set the local values to match Compose: `DB_HOST=pgsql`, `DB_PORT=5432`, `DB_DATABASE=laravel`, `DB_USERNAME=sail`, `DB_PASSWORD=password`. These are local demo values only.

3. Build and start the app and PostgreSQL containers:

   ```bash
   ./vendor/bin/sail up -d --build
   ```

4. Create the Laravel app key, database tables, and made-up demo accounts/data; then build the browser assets:

   ```bash
   ./vendor/bin/sail artisan key:generate
   ./vendor/bin/sail artisan migrate --seed
   ./vendor/bin/sail npm install
   ./vendor/bin/sail npm run build
   ```

5. Open `http://localhost` in Windows or Ubuntu. Sign in with one of the local-only demo accounts in `README.md`.
6. When done, stop the containers:

   ```bash
   ./vendor/bin/sail down
   ```

## 5. How to test the main workflow locally

1. Sign in as the demo teacher and open appointments.
2. Create or view a request for the demo student and choose an available time.
3. Sign in as the demo admin and check the request, change its status, and open the demo case and follow-up.
4. Sign in as the demo student and confirm the student view only shows that student's appointment information.
5. For API checks, see the endpoint list in `README.md`; use only the local demo accounts and local database.

## 6. Prepare a Render test deploy

The repo now has a `render.yaml` Blueprint. A **Blueprint** is a setup file telling Render to create the app service and PostgreSQL database with the right connection. It uses the repo's Dockerfile, `/up` health check, PHP 8.5, and PostgreSQL 18. Automatic online demo seeding is disabled.

Before deploying:

1. Make sure Docker can build the image locally if possible:

   ```bash
   docker build -t guidancesched-render-test .
   ```

2. Commit the deployment files and push them to a GitHub branch your Render account can access. Never commit `.env`, a real password, or an `APP_KEY`.
3. In Render, choose **New → Blueprint**, connect the GitHub repo, and select the branch containing `render.yaml`.
4. Render will show the app and database it plans to create. Select the free test plans if offered, review the resources, then apply/create them.
5. When prompted for `APP_KEY`, paste a fresh Laravel key. Generate one on a PHP 8.4+ machine from the project folder with:

   ```bash
   php artisan key:generate --show
   ```

   If you cannot run Artisan locally, generate a key using the deployed container shell after it is built, then enter it in Render's environment settings and redeploy. Keep the key private and do not change it after real encrypted data or user sessions exist.
6. The Blueprint connects `APP_URL` and `ASSET_URL` to the HTTPS URL Render gives the service.
7. Wait for the deploy to show **Live** and the `/up` health check to pass. Open the service URL and confirm the login page loads.
8. Create a test admin account in Render's service shell with `php artisan tinker`, using a new password only for the test deployment. For example, in Tinker run:

   ```php
   \App\Models\User::create([
       'name' => 'Test Admin',
       'email' => 'your-email@example.com',
       'role' => 'admin',
       'password' => \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Hash::make('your-new-test-password'),
   ]);
   ```

   Do not use the public demo password. The deployed container intentionally does not seed demo users.
9. Sign in and try one appointment flow using fictional data. Check the Render logs if the page or database connection fails.

Free Render web services can go idle and take time to wake up. Free Render PostgreSQL is temporary and expires after 30 days, so this is only a short-lived test environment. Use fictional data only. Review the current [Render Laravel and Docker guide](https://render.com/docs/deploy-php-laravel-docker), [Blueprint guide](https://render.com/docs/blueprint-spec), and [Render PostgreSQL guide](https://render.com/docs/postgresql-creating-connecting) while setting it up.

## 7. What the deployment files do

- `Dockerfile` builds the CSS/JavaScript files, installs Laravel's production PHP packages, configures Apache on Render's web port, runs database migrations, and starts the website.
- `render.yaml` tells Render to make the test web service and PostgreSQL database, link them with a private database address, and check `/up` to see whether the site is running.
- `.env` is for local settings only. On Render, set private values in the Render dashboard rather than adding them to Git.
- `database/seeders/DatabaseSeeder.php` is for fictional local demo records; run `migrate --seed` locally, not as part of the public Render startup.

## 8. What “test deploy” means here

A test deploy means putting a temporary copy online and checking that it starts, connects to PostgreSQL, shows the login page, and completes a basic appointment workflow with made-up records. It does not prove that the website is ready for real student information or that it can handle production traffic.

# R7 Performance Test

## Scope and method

This plan uses ApacheBench (`ab`) against the REST API from R2. It covers one read transaction (`GET /api/appointments`) and one write transaction (`POST /api/appointments`). The write endpoint requires an administrator account and a valid synthetic student ID.

Run this only against a disposable local database populated with synthetic records. Each successful write creates an appointment, so restore or discard that database after the experiment. Do not run the write workload against a shared or production database.

Set the base URL and synthetic credentials in the shell. `R7_STUDENT_ID` must identify a student in the test database. `R7_REQUESTS` is 300 for every run below, which gives each run enough samples to report the p95 latency while keeping the write count controlled.

```sh
export R7_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1
export R7_ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@guidancesched.test
export R7_ADMIN_PASSWORD='ChangeMe123!'
export R7_STUDENT_ID=3
export R7_REQUESTS=300
```

Create the request body file for ApacheBench:

```sh
cat > /tmp/r7-appointment.json <<EOF
{"student_id":${R7_STUDENT_ID},"title":"R7 synthetic load test","reason":"Synthetic performance test"}
EOF
```

Run each transaction at concurrency 1, 10, and 50. Save each complete output to a separate file so the summary values can be transcribed into the results table.

```sh
for concurrency in 1 10 50; do
    ab -n "$R7_REQUESTS" -c "$concurrency" \
        -A "$R7_ADMIN_EMAIL:$R7_ADMIN_PASSWORD" \
        -H 'Accept: application/json' \
        "$R7_BASE_URL/api/appointments" \
        > "r7-read-c${concurrency}.txt" 2>&1
done

for concurrency in 1 10 50; do
    ab -n "$R7_REQUESTS" -c "$concurrency" \
        -A "$R7_ADMIN_EMAIL:$R7_ADMIN_PASSWORD" \
        -H 'Accept: application/json' \
        -T 'application/json' \
        -p /tmp/r7-appointment.json \
        "$R7_BASE_URL/api/appointments" \
        > "r7-write-c${concurrency}.txt" 2>&1
done
```

For each output, record `Requests per second`, `Time per request` (mean), `95%` latency, and `Failed requests`. Check the HTTP status counts as well: a run with authentication or validation failures is not a successful performance result. For this API, successful list requests return 200 and creates return 201. Since `ab` repeats the same POST body, all created rows are synthetic and must be discarded with the test database after the run.

## Environment

| Item | Observed value |
| --- | --- |
| Host CPU | 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12500H; 16 logical CPUs (8 cores) |
| Host memory | 7.6 GiB total; approximately 4.4 GiB available when inspected |
| Runtime stack | Laravel Sail, PHP 8.5 application container, PostgreSQL 18 Alpine container |
| Container CPU/memory limits | None declared in `compose.yaml` |
| Load tool | ApacheBench (`ab`); present at `/usr/bin/ab` |
| Application state at report preparation | Not running; Docker or Podman daemon unavailable |

Host memory availability is a point-in-time observation and may change. Container allocation is unrestricted by Compose, so report the host limits and do not claim a smaller per-container allocation.

## Results

The six ApacheBench runs completed on 2026-11-26. Each run sent 300 requests. ApacheBench reported zero failed requests for all runs, giving a measured failure rate of 0%. Follow-up checks confirmed that the read endpoint returns HTTP 200 and the write endpoint returns HTTP 201.

| Transaction | Concurrency | Requests | Throughput (req/s) | Mean (ms) | p95 (ms) | Failed / error rate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Read: list appointments | 1 | 300 | 3.31 | 301.8 | 356 | 0 / 0% |
| Read: list appointments | 10 | 300 | 16.53 | 604.8 | 947 | 0 / 0% |
| Read: list appointments | 50 | 300 | 13.35 | 3,745.7 | 4,609 | 0 / 0% |
| Write: create appointment | 1 | 300 | 3.39 | 295.4 | 338 | 0 / 0% |
| Write: create appointment | 10 | 300 | 15.00 | 666.7 | 943 | 0 / 0% |
| Write: create appointment | 50 | 300 | 14.94 | 3,347.6 | 4,063 | 0 / 0% |

## Interpretation

Performance begins to degrade between concurrency 10 and 50. Read throughput falls from 16.53 to 13.35 requests per second, while mean response time rises from 604.8 ms to 3,745.7 ms and p95 from 947 ms to 4,609 ms. Write throughput is nearly flat, changing from 15.00 to 14.94 requests per second, while mean response time rises from 666.7 ms to 3,347.6 ms and p95 from 943 ms to 4,063 ms. All runs report zero failed requests.

The similar slowdown in both reads and writes points to contention in shared capacity, most likely the application and/or database tier. The measurements do not isolate which one: CPU, memory, database activity, and application worker utilization were not recorded during the runs. Collecting those measurements during a repeat would be needed to identify a specific bottleneck. Throughput and latency alone are evidence of saturation under 50 concurrent connections, not proof of which component caused it.

    <script>
        document.getElementById('toggle-password')?.addEventListener('click', function () {
            const password = document.getElementById(this.getAttribute('aria-controls'));
            const isVisible = password.type === 'text';
            password.type = isVisible ? 'password' : 'text';
            this.textContent = isVisible ? 'Show' : 'Hide';
            this.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(!isVisible));
            this.setAttribute('aria-label', isVisible ? 'Show password' : 'Hide password');
        });
    </script>

<script>
    const mobileMenuToggle = document.querySelector('.mobile-menu-toggle');
    const appNavigation = document.querySelector('.app-sidebar');
    mobileMenuToggle?.addEventListener('click', () => {
        const isOpen = appNavigation.classList.toggle('is-open');
        mobileMenuToggle.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(isOpen));
        mobileMenuToggle.setAttribute('aria-label', isOpen ? 'Close navigation menu' : 'Open navigation menu');
        mobileMenuToggle.textContent = isOpen ? '×' : '☰';
    });
    document.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
        if (event.key === 'Escape' && appNavigation?.classList.contains('is-open')) {
            appNavigation.classList.remove('is-open');
            mobileMenuToggle?.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
            mobileMenuToggle?.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Open navigation menu');
            if (mobileMenuToggle) mobileMenuToggle.textContent = '☰';
            mobileMenuToggle?.focus();
        }
    });

    window.setupAvailableSlotPicker = function (dateSelect, timeSelect, endpoint, selectedTime = '', requireSelection = false, appointmentId = null) {
        let requestNumber = 0;
        const refresh = async () => {
            const currentRequest = ++requestNumber;
            const date = dateSelect.value;
            const previousSelection = selectedTime || timeSelect.value;
            timeSelect.replaceChildren(new Option('Choose a time', ''));
            timeSelect.disabled = true;
            timeSelect.required = requireSelection || Boolean(date);
            if (!date) return;

            const params = new URLSearchParams({ date });
            if (appointmentId) params.set('appointment_id', appointmentId);
            try {
                const response = await fetch(`${endpoint}?${params}`, { headers: { Accept: 'application/json' }, cache: 'no-store' });
                if (currentRequest !== requestNumber || dateSelect.value !== date) return;
                if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
                const { times } = await response.json();
                if (currentRequest !== requestNumber || dateSelect.value !== date) return;
                if (times.length === 0) timeSelect.options[0].text = 'No open times for this date';
                times.forEach((time) => timeSelect.add(new Option(time.label, time.value, false, time.value === previousSelection)));
                timeSelect.disabled = false;
                selectedTime = '';
            } catch (error) {
                if (currentRequest !== requestNumber) return;
                timeSelect.replaceChildren(new Option(`Unable to load available times${error.message ? ` (${error.message})` : ''}`, ''));
            }
        };
        dateSelect.addEventListener('change', () => {
            selectedTime = '';
            refresh();
        });
        refresh();
    };
</script>

<?php

use App\Http\Controllers\Api\GuidanceApiController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

// These routes send JSON data to another program instead of returning Blade web pages.
// HTTP Basic authentication keeps this small prototype API stateless.
// The API controller still performs role and record-ownership checks after authentication succeeds.
Route::middleware('auth.basic')->group(function () {
    // Appointment API: list, create, view, update, cancel, and delete requests.
    Route::get('/appointments', [GuidanceApiController::class, 'appointments']);
    Route::post('/appointments', [GuidanceApiController::class, 'createAppointment']);
    Route::get('/appointments/{appointment}', [GuidanceApiController::class, 'showAppointment']);
    Route::patch('/appointments/{appointment}', [GuidanceApiController::class, 'updateAppointment']);
    Route::patch('/appointments/{appointment}/cancel', [GuidanceApiController::class, 'cancelAppointment']);

# Security best practices

## Control mass assignment

Define ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___$fillable___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ when a model is populated from request-derived arrays, or deliberately guard attributes by another consistent model convention. Laravel models guard all attributes by default. ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___$guarded = []___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ opts out of that protection.

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
class User extends Model
{
    protected $fillable = [
        'name',
        'email',
        'password',
    ];
}
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

Do not pass untrusted request data to a model with ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___$guarded = []___SINGLE_BACKTICK___. Mass-assignment protection controls which attributes ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___create()___SINGLE_BACKTICK___, ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___fill()___SINGLE_BACKTICK___, and ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___update()___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ may set. It does not validate values or authorize the operation.

## Authorize protected actions

Use policies, gates, or form request authorization for actions that depend on the current user's permissions. Authentication alone does not establish permission, and validation is not authorization.

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
public function update(UpdatePostRequest $request, Post $post): RedirectResponse
{
    Gate::authorize('update', $post);

    $post->update($request->validated());

    return redirect()->route('posts.show', $post);
}
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

Authorization may instead live in the form request:

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
public function authorize(): bool
{
    return $this->user()?->can('update', $this->route('post')) ?? false;
}
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

Public actions intentionally available to everyone do not need a redundant authorization check.

## Bind query parameters

Use Eloquent, the query builder, or explicit bindings instead of interpolating untrusted values into Structured Query Language (SQL). Bindings protect values, not identifiers such as column names or sort directions. Map user-selected identifiers to an allow-list.

Incorrect:

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
DB::select("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{$request->name}'");
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

Correct:

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
User::where('name', $request->name)->get();
User::whereRaw('LOWER(name) = ?', [$request->string('name')->lower()->toString()])->get();
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

## Escape output in its context

Blade's ___SINGLE_BACKTICK______BLADE_ESCAPE_2______SINGLE_BACKTICK___ syntax HTML-escapes output. Use ___SINGLE_BACKTICK______BLADE_ESCAPE_0______SINGLE_BACKTICK___ only for content sanitized for the exact HTML context where it renders. Escaping rules differ for HTML, URLs, JavaScript, and Cascading Style Sheets.

Incorrect for untrusted content:

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___blade
___BLADE_ESCAPE_1___
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

Correct:

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___blade
___BLADE_ESCAPE_3___
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

## Apply cross-site request forgery protection

Include ___SINGLE_BACKTICK______BLADE_ESCAPE_4___csrf___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ in state-changing Blade forms handled by Laravel's ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___web___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ middleware. Routes intentionally excluded from cross-site request forgery (CSRF) verification, such as validated third-party webhooks, need their own authenticity check.

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___blade
<form method="POST" action="/posts">
    ___BLADE_ESCAPE_5___csrf
    <input type="text" name="title">
</form>
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

Inertia applications commonly use Axios, which returns the encrypted ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___XSRF-TOKEN___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ cookie in the ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___X-XSRF-TOKEN___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ header. When you use another HTTP client, confirm equivalent configuration. Do not disable CSRF protection only to fix a token mismatch.

## Rate limit sensitive endpoints

Apply suitable rate limits to login attempts, password recovery, verification messages, and expensive or abuse-prone application programming interface (API) routes. Choose the limiter key deliberately. An Internet Protocol (IP) address alone can unfairly group users behind a shared network. An account identifier alone can enable targeted denial of service.

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
RateLimiter::for('login', function (Request $request) {
    return Limit::perMinute(5)->by(Str::transliterate(
        Str::lower($request->string('email')).'|'.$request->ip()
    ));
});

Route::post('/login', LoginController::class)->middleware('throttle:login');
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

Rate limiting reduces abuse. It does not replace authentication, authorization, or upstream denial-of-service protection.

## Validate and store uploads safely

Validate the expected content type, the size, and the dimensions where relevant. Laravel's ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___mimes___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ rule reads the file contents and guesses a Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) type corresponding to the listed extensions. It does not validate the user-assigned filename extension. The ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___extensions___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ rule checks that extension. Do not use it by itself.

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
public function rules(): array
{
    return [
        'avatar' => ['required', 'image', 'mimes:jpg,jpeg,png,webp', 'max:2048'],
    ];
}
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

Use Laravel's storage methods to generate a filename, and store untrusted files outside a publicly executable location. Public files can require additional controls, such as image re-encoding, content-disposition headers, and explicit blocking of active formats.

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
$path = $request->file('avatar')->store('avatars');
___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

## Keep secrets out of application code

Do not commit populated environment files or hard-code credentials. Read environment variables in configuration files, then use ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___config()___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ in application code so configuration caching works. See the configuration rules for encrypted environment files and external secret stores.

## Audit dependencies

Run ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___<?php echo e($assist->composerCommand('audit')); ?>___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ regularly and in continuous integration. Review findings for exploitability and update or mitigate affected packages promptly.

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___bash
<?php echo e($assist->composerCommand('audit')); ?>

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___

## Encrypt sensitive attributes when appropriate

Use an ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___encrypted___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ cast for sensitive values that must be recoverable, and use ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___$hidden___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ to omit them from array and JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) serialization. Hidden attributes remain accessible in PHP, and encryption does not replace access control. You cannot meaningfully query encrypted values. Store them in a ___SINGLE_BACKTICK___TEXT___SINGLE_BACKTICK___ or larger column because ciphertext length varies.

___SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK______SINGLE_BACKTICK___php
class Integration extends Model
{
    protected $hidden = ['api_key', 'api_secret'];

    protected function casts(): array
    {
        return [
            'api_key' => 'encrypted',
            'api_secret' => 'encrypted',
        ];
    }
}
